lesson.title: Finding the Finish Line: Final Conditions in RL and RC Circuits
lesson.summary: Final conditions are the values that inductor current or capacitor voltage settle to as time goes to infinity, found by treating inductors as short circuits and capacitors as open circuits in the new steady state. They supply one of the two boundary values needed to fully solve any first-order transient circuit.
lesson.body:
Solving an RL or RC circuit after a switch changes state always comes down to filling in the same template: response(t) = final value + (initial value minus final value) times e^(-t/tau). Two of those three ingredients, the initial value and the final value, are not found by solving a differential equation at all; they come from ordinary DC circuit analysis applied at two different moments in time. The final value, specifically, is what circuit texts call the final condition, and getting it right is often the difference between a correct answer and a wrong one, because a sign or magnitude error here propagates through the entire solution.

Final conditions rely on the same steady-state trick introduced earlier: once a very long time has passed after a switching event, capacitor voltage and inductor current stop changing, so a capacitor behaves like an open circuit and an inductor behaves like a plain wire, or short circuit. To find the final value of any inductor current or capacitor voltage, redraw the circuit with that substitution made, using the source and resistor values that apply after the switch has moved to its new position, and then solve the resulting resistive circuit with Ohm's Law and Kirchhoff's Laws.

Take a series RL circuit where a switch connects a 20 V source through a 5 ohm resistor to an inductor L. Before the switch closes, no current flows, so i(0) = 0 A. That is the initial condition. After the switch has been closed for a long time, the inductor has settled into steady state and behaves as a short circuit, so it contributes zero resistance to the loop. The final current is simply i(infinity) = V/R = 20 V / 5 ohms = 4 A. That 4 A is the final condition, and it is exactly the value the current is heading toward no matter what path the transient takes to get there.

An RC circuit works the same way with the substitution flipped. Take a 24 V source feeding a 2 kilo-ohm resistor in series, which then splits into a 4 kilo-ohm resistor in parallel with a capacitor. At steady state, the capacitor draws no current, so it behaves as an open circuit and the final capacitor voltage is set by a plain voltage divider across the two resistors: V_C(infinity) = 24 V x (4 k / (2 k + 4 k)) = 24 V x (4/6) = 16 V. Notice this final condition calculation is identical in method to the steady-state response example worked earlier, just applied specifically to identify one of the two boundary values a transient solution needs.

Once you have both the initial condition (found from the circuit just before switching, or from a stated starting charge or flux) and the final condition (found from the circuit long after switching, using the open-capacitor and shorted-inductor substitutions), the exponential decay term connecting them is determined entirely by the time constant. Final conditions are therefore not a side calculation, they are half of the entire answer, and every step response and complete response problem you encounter next depends on getting this half right first.
